---
title: "Findings"
subtitle: "What the data said, including where it contradicted itself"
---

## The correlation trap

The three strongest relationships in this dataset are **non-monotonic**, and in
all three the correlation coefficient misleads.

`num_of_products` spans 92 points between groups — from 7.6% churn at two
products to 100% at four — and its Spearman correlation with churn is **−0.05**.
A feature selection step filtering on |ρ| > 0.1 would have deleted the strongest
predictor in the table.

The reason is mechanical. Correlation measures monotonicity. Risk falls from one
product to two and then explodes at three and four; averaged over the range, the
ups cancel the downs.

::: {.thread}
This is already an argument about model choice, made before any model existed. A
linear model has to be told about a shape like this. A tree finds it alone.
:::

## The finding that changed the conclusion

Exploration first established that age describes an inverted U: risk climbs to
the 50-59 band and falls after. **That turned out to be a composition artefact.**

```{python}
#| label: fig-interaction
#| fig-cap: "Split by activity, the inverted U disappears. Among inactive customers risk never stops climbing; among active ones it does fall after 60. The aggregate curve only bends because the share of active customers changes across age bands."
import charts
charts.age_activity()
```

Two consequences follow, and both are decisions rather than observations.

**On modelling.** A model that treats age additively cannot represent this. It
has to capture an interaction — an argument for trees over linear models, made
from the data rather than from preference.

**On the business.** The highest-risk cell in the whole dataset is *inactive and
over 60*. And activity is the one variable the bank can actually change. Age is
observed; inactivity is fought.

## The confounder that halved an effect

Customers with zero balance churn at 13.8% against 24.1% for those with a
balance — a gap of 10.3 points, and it looks conclusive.

Except **Germany has not one single customer with zero balance**, and Germany
churns at 32.4%. Every German sits in the "has a balance" bucket, dragging it up.

Removing Germany, the gap falls to **4.9 points**. The effect is real and half the
size it looked. Reporting the 10.3 would not have been a lie, but it would have
been wrong — and nobody would have caught it without the country breakdown.

## Four signs the data is synthetic

None of these was looked for. All four turned up pulling on a quality check.

| | Signal | Why it gives the game away |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Salary with skew 0.00 and kurtosis −1.18 | The exact values of a uniform distribution. Real salaries pile up low with a long right tail |
| 2 | Age and tenure correlate at −0.01 | In real data tenure grows with age. These were drawn independently |
| 3 | All 60 customers with four products left | 100% across sixty cases is a rule, not a behaviour |
| 4 | No outlier possible in salary | In a uniform distribution the interquartile fences fall outside the data by construction |

The second explains the 322 accounts apparently opened before the customer turned
18. There are no corrupt rows to clean: the generator rolled one die for age and
another for tenure, and some combinations came out impossible.

::: {.note}
**The honest implication.** The interactions a model can learn here are limited to
the ones the generator introduced. Detecting that from the internal
inconsistencies is worth more than repeating that it is "a clean dataset of ten
thousand rows with no nulls".
:::

## Two effects with no available explanation

Germany churns at twice the rate of France and Spain while being
**indistinguishable on every observable variable** — same mean age, same share of
active customers, same product counts. Women churn at 25.1% against 16.5% for
men, and the gap replicates inside all three countries.

Both variables predict well **precisely because they stand in for something not
measured**. That is what makes them dangerous rather than useful, and it is why
the deployed model does not use gender.
